headline_result_summary: Exploiting the timing of local administrative jurisdiction splitting (pemekaran) across Indonesian districts from 2001 to 2010, Lewis (2017) finds that local government proliferation negatively affects household access to protected water and sanitation relative to original districts, contradicting claims that bringing government closer to citizens via smaller jurisdictions improves service delivery. In the author's preferred dynamic difference-GMM specification comparing newly created districts to all original districts (N = 2,693 across 336 district groups, Table 5), lagged new district formation reduces combined household protected water and sanitation access by 1.351 percentage points in the second year of operations (SE = 0.584, p < 0.05), implying a long-run reduction of approximately 1.75 percentage points (p = .023); in the corresponding static FE model with district-specific time trends (N = 2,714, Table 4), the lagged effect is −0.987 percentage points (SE = 0.579, p < 0.10). However, contemporaneous year-1 effects are null across all models, and when the control group is restricted solely to the 98 ever-splitting districts before they split (Split vs. new, N = 750 static / 733 dynamic), neither static nor dynamic estimates show any statistically significant difference in water and sanitation access.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Exposure orientation / theory-expectation reversal trap: Local government proliferation (splitting districts into smaller subnational units to bring government closer to citizens) is framed by decentralization advocates as a pro-citizen governance reform, yet its empirical impact on household water and sanitation access is negative (unfavorable_to_access). If a synthesis instead defines the desirable pole as jurisdictional consolidation or avoiding administrative fragmentation, the valence would invert; coders must explicitly anchor to the author's coded exposure (New district = 1 post-split vs. 0 unsplit). 2. Comparator-group sensitivity: The negative effect holds only when comparing new districts against the full set of 336 original districts (including 238 never-split districts); when comparing post-split against pre-split observations solely within the 98 splitting districts ('Split vs. new' in Tables 4 and 5), all water/sanitation estimates are statistically null (−0.162 and −0.923 in static FE; 0.024 and −0.690 in dynamic GMM). 3. Lag structure and p-value threshold: In every specification, the contemporaneous 'New district' indicator is near zero and non-significant, and deeper lags beyond 1 year are also reported as null; the effect appears specifically on 'Lagged new district' (second year of operations), where the static FE DiD model with district-specific time trends is only significant at p < 0.10 (−0.987, SE = 0.579*) while the dynamic difference-GMM model (which drops district-specific trends) is significant at p < 0.05 (−1.351, SE = 0.584**; long-run −1.75%, p = .023). 4. Composite outcome definition: 'Infrastructure access' is the unweighted district average of % households with protected water and % households with protected sanitation (from SUSENAS), rather than piped water or sanitation separately.
study_design: Longitudinal panel quasi-experimental study (2001–2010) using static generalized difference-in-differences (two-way fixed effects with district-specific linear time trends) and dynamic panel two-step difference-GMM (Arellano-Bond), exploiting plausibly exogenous timing of administrative district splits (including a 2004–2006 central moratorium and parliamentary vetting delays)
unit_and_sample_size: Indonesian districts (kabupaten/kota, excluding Jakarta) collapsed into consistent 2001 original district boundaries: 336 original district groups (238 never-split districts and 98 split districts that formed 253 new parent/child districts over 2001–2010). Analytic sample sizes for water/sanitation infrastructure regressions: N = 2,714 district-year observations (static FE) and N = 2,693 district-year observations (dynamic GMM) across 336 district groups in the Original vs. new comparison; N = 750 district-year observations (static FE) and N = 733 district-year observations (dynamic GMM) across 98 district groups in the Split vs. new comparison.
